Appendix A Related Work

Our work sits at the intersection of long-horizon agent control, safety, and structured policy representations. The key distinction is policy externalization: instead of improving an implicit, transcript-driven controller, we distill a single executable artifact from aggregate experience and then execute traversal as the policy whenever in coverage.

Improving intrinsic reasoning and memory.

A large body of work strengthens agent performance by amplifying internal reasoning. Deliberative methods such as Tree-of-Thoughts (ToT) (Yao et al., 2023) expand online search, often at substantial inference cost. Self-improvement approaches such as Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) and Meta-Policy Reflexion (Wu et al., 2025) store textual “reflection memories” to adapt from failures. These techniques remain fundamentally generation-centric: they either operate online or build non-executable textual memories, and the long-horizon policy is still realized through unconstrained language generation conditioned on a growing transcript. In contrast, our framework distills both successes (for behavioral guidance) and failures (for safety) into a single offline, executable structure; the resulting controller is an inspectable artifact whose traversal determines the executed macro skeleton in covered episodes.

Guardrailing and runtime validation.

The dominant safety paradigm for agents is “guardrailing”: attach a runtime validator, critic, or guardian agent that checks actions as they are proposed (Xiang et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2025; Kholkar and Ahuja, 2025). While effective in reducing harm, these systems typically rely on human-specified policies (natural-language rules, prompt templates, or code), which is unscalable and often misses the long tail of emergent, context-dependent failure modes that appear only in operational data. Our approach flips the source of safety knowledge: we deterministically replay unsafe traces, shrink them to minimal violating windows, and compile the resulting structured contexts into pre-execution gates that are grounded in observed failures. This converts failure logs into a growing, executable safety mechanism rather than a passive record.

Formal guarantees, learned constraints, and the safety–utility trade-off.

Formal methods such as shielding (Könighofer et al., 2025) can offer strong verifiable guarantees, but they typically require manually crafted formal environment models, an intractable prerequisite for most open-world agent tasks. Hybrid approaches that learn probabilistic models online (Koohestani, 2025) can provide only probabilistic assurances, whereas our gates provide deterministic checks over structured tool contexts. Other paradigms internalize safety via implicit optimization trade-offs, such as Constrained MDPs (CMDPs) (Gu et al., 2024) or adversarial training (Debenedetti et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025b). These methods embed safety inside an opaque, monolithic policy, making it difficult to inspect or certify what constraints are enforced and where. Our framework instead externalizes safety into an explicit library of deterministic predicates over structured contexts, and enforces an experience-grounded monotonicity rule: once a context is observed unsafe and rejected, it cannot be re-admitted by later updates. This yields a verifiable notion of non-regression on observed unsafe contexts while still allowing behavioral improvement through coverage expansion.

Structured policy representations for agents.

Hierarchical controllers such as finite state machines (FSMs) (Liu et al., 2024; Crouse et al., 2024) and behavior trees (BTs) (Wang et al., 2025a; Izzo et al., 2025) offer interpretability and modularity, but are often hand-crafted by experts or generated once from a single high-level instruction. This “Policy-as-Code” paradigm is brittle under distribution shift and typically lacks a principled link between operational failures and controller updates. Our approach is “Policy-as-Data”: we distill a Gated Behavior Tree from massive aggregate experience, merge-checking macros to avoid semantic aliasing where safety matters, attaching node-local gates from unsafe windows, and executing traversal as the policy within an explicit coverage boundary. The result is not a one-off plan for a single instruction, but a reusable policy artifact that unifies behavioral guidance, deterministic pre-execution safety, recovery, and long-horizon memory within a single executable structure.

Appendix B Safety Specification, Structured Contexts, and the Global Guardrail

B.1 Normative Safety Specification in OpenHands and Sandboxed Data

What is normative safety 𝒮spec\mathcal{S}_{\text{spec}}?

All trajectories are executed inside the OpenHands runtime, which provides (i) a Docker-isolated sandbox, (ii) a standardized event stream of tool actions and observations, and (iii) benchmark-defined checkers plus runtime monitors that emit verdicts. Together, monitors and checkers define a normative safety specification 𝒮spec\mathcal{S}_{\text{spec}} over primitive tool calls: a primitive violates 𝒮spec\mathcal{S}_{\text{spec}} iff at execution time it triggers any monitor or checker safety verdict. Examples include (non-exhaustive): writes outside workspace roots, deletion of protected directories, process spawn patterns disallowed by the sandbox policy, network traffic to disallowed destinations, and benchmark-specific leakage/exfiltration triggers.

Trajectory labeling.

A trajectory τ\tau is labeled unsafe iff at least one executed primitive violates 𝒮spec\mathcal{S}_{\text{spec}} under the OpenHands monitors/checkers. This is the only ground-truth safety label used throughout the pipeline.

Design goal (coverage-scoped claims).

We do not claim complete enforcement of 𝒮spec\mathcal{S}_{\text{spec}} for all hazards. Instead, we externalize and deterministically enforce an executable bounded-history subset (defined below) and treat violations under the current system as evidence that expands this executable subset monotonically over observed unsafe contexts (Design invariant 1).

B.2 Structured Contexts: The Only Inputs to Gates

Structured context schema.

For each candidate high-risk primitive, we construct a structured context ctx∈𝒞\texttt{ctx}\in\mathcal{C} directly from sandbox state. The gate library reads only these structured fields and a bounded history of recent high-risk primitives; it never reads LLM summaries, chain-of-thought, or free-form transcripts. Concretely, we represent ctx as:

ctx = { primitive_type, tool_family, args, resource_ids,
workspace_roots, cwd, uid/gid,
net_dest(domain, ip, port, scheme),
proc_meta(exec, argv, parent),
payload_meta(len, mime, hash),
recent_hard_history[1..H]}

where: (i) args/resource_ids store canonicalized file paths (normalized, resolved, and checked against sandbox roots), URL components (domain/scheme/path), and process identifiers where applicable; (ii) payload_meta stores metadata for payload-bearing actions (length, MIME/type if known, and a stable hash); and (iii) recent_hard_history records the last HH high-risk primitives within the same macro, each stored as a compact structured record (type, canonical_resource, coarse_op, timestamp). We use a fixed small history bound H=4H=4 in the reference configuration.

High-risk primitive set 𝒯hard\mathcal{T}_{\text{hard}}.

We designate as high-risk:

𝒯hard={all writes and deletes}∪{all process spawns}∪{all network sends}∪{reads matching sensitive patterns}.\mathcal{T}_{\text{hard}}=\{\text{all writes and deletes}\}\cup\{\text{all process spawns}\}\cup\{\text{all network sends}\}\cup\{\text{reads matching sensitive patterns}\}.

The sensitive patterns component is benchmark- and runtime-aware and includes protected filesystem prefixes, environment/key material patterns, and benchmark-defined secret resources (when applicable).

Non-bypassability.

Because ctx is constructed from sandbox state and canonicalization is deterministic, no prompting or summarization choice can alter gate inputs. Summaries may influence how a macro is realized, but cannot change ctx nor the outcome of deterministic gates computed from it.

B.3 Gate Interface, Global vs. Node-Local Gates, and Executable Safety Subset

Gate interface (common to all gate families).

Every gate has the same interface:

g:ctx↦(ok,msg)∈{true,false}×String.g:\ \texttt{ctx}\mapsto(\texttt{ok},\texttt{msg})\in\{\texttt{true},\texttt{false}\}\times\texttt{String}.

We write 𝒢global​(t)\mathcal{G}_{\text{global}}(t) for global gates and 𝒢node​(t)\mathcal{G}_{\text{node}}(t) for node-local gates attached to macros in the tree, and 𝒢⁡(t)=𝒢global​(t)∪𝒢node​(t)\mathcal{G}(t)=\mathcal{G}_{\text{global}}(t)\cup\mathcal{G}_{\text{node}}(t).

Executable safety subset.

We define the executable subset at time tt as:

𝒮sys(t)={ctx∈𝒞:∃g∈𝒢(t)s.t.g(ctx).ok=false}.\mathcal{S}_{\text{sys}}(t)=\left\{\texttt{ctx}\in\mathcal{C}:\exists g\in\mathcal{G}(t)\ \text{s.t.}\ g(\texttt{ctx}).\texttt{ok}=\texttt{false}\right\}.

This is a conservative, bounded-history approximation of the portion of 𝒮spec\mathcal{S}_{\text{spec}} that is expressible via structured contexts.

Global decision (always-on, pre-execution).

For any candidate high-risk primitive a∈𝒯harda\in\mathcal{T}_{\text{hard}}:

HardGateOK​(a,ctx)=⋀g∈𝒢globalg⁡(ctx).ok.\texttt{HardGateOK}(a,\texttt{ctx})=\bigwedge_{g\in\mathcal{G}_{\text{global}}}g(\texttt{ctx}).\texttt{ok}.

This check runs before execution for every high-risk primitive in every phase: data collection, offline distillation, and online deployment.

Node-local decision (macro-scoped, pre-execution).

When a macro node vv is selected during traversal/recovery, we additionally enforce:

GateOK​(v,ctx)=⋀g∈𝒢⁡(v)g⁡(ctx).ok.\texttt{GateOK}(v,\texttt{ctx})=\bigwedge_{g\in\mathcal{G}(v)}g(\texttt{ctx}).\texttt{ok}.

The executed primitive is allowed only if both global and node-local checks pass (as in Sec. 2.5).

B.4 Gate Families: Deterministic RuleGates and Deterministic ContentGates

RuleGates (fully deterministic).

RuleGates are pure code predicates over structured fields in ctx and its bounded history, for example: (i) forbid writes outside workspace roots; (ii) forbid deletion of protected paths; (iii) forbid process spawn patterns (e.g., executing disallowed binaries); (iv) forbid network sends to disallowed domains/ports; and (v) block short-window structured patterns such as “read sensitive resource then archive then send” when all components are detectable from ctx and bounded history. RuleGates are unit-tested and deterministic.

ContentGates (deterministic calls to a frozen classifier).

Some hazards are primarily carried by unstructured payloads (text/code/serialized blobs). For payload-bearing actions, ContentGates construct a guard prompt from: (i) ctx structured fields, (ii) a short payload excerpt or redacted summary, (iii) a task/macro tag), then call a frozen safety classifier at temperature 00 and post-process into a boolean decision. In the reference configuration we use Llama-Guard-3-8B at temperature 00 as the classifier (see App. I.2).

Determinism contract.

ContentGates are deterministic conditional on (i) a fixed guard model, (ii) temperature 00, and (iii) a fixed prompt template. They do not introduce stochasticity into enforcement.

B.5 Experience-Grounded Corpora and Monotone Updates (No Unsafe Re-Admission)

Unsafe and benign corpora.

For each gate gg we maintain:

  • •

    an unsafe corpus 𝒟unsafe​(g)\mathcal{D}_{\text{unsafe}}(g): structured contexts extracted from trajectories that violate 𝒮spec\mathcal{S}_{\text{spec}} (minimal windows, App. E);

  • •

    a benign corpus 𝒟benign​(g)\mathcal{D}_{\text{benign}}(g): representative safe contexts of the same primitive family (same tool family, same risk class) sampled from successful or non-violating runs.

We maintain balanced benign sampling across resource types and macro neighborhoods to avoid overfitting gates to a narrow distribution.

Update rule (monotonicity + benign regression control).

Any update from goldg^{\text{old}} to gnewg^{\text{new}} must satisfy:

∀ctx∈𝒟unsafe(g):gold(ctx).ok=false⇒gnew(ctx).ok=false,\forall\,\texttt{ctx}\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{unsafe}}(g):\quad g^{\text{old}}(\texttt{ctx}).\texttt{ok}=\texttt{false}\Rightarrow g^{\text{new}}(\texttt{ctx}).\texttt{ok}=\texttt{false},

and limit benign false positives:

|{ctx∈𝒟benign(g):gnew(ctx).ok=false}||𝒟benign​(g)|≤ϵbenign.\frac{\left|\left\{\texttt{ctx}\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{benign}}(g):g^{\text{new}}(\texttt{ctx}).\texttt{ok}=\texttt{false}\right\}\right|}{|\mathcal{D}_{\text{benign}}(g)|}\leq\epsilon_{\text{benign}}.

In the reference configuration we use ϵbenign=0.01\epsilon_{\text{benign}}=0.01 for global gates and ϵbenign=0.02\epsilon_{\text{benign}}=0.02 for node-local gates (node-local gates are intentionally allowed to be slightly more conservative within a macro neighborhood).

Design invariant 1 (Experience-grounded monotonicity).

Once a structured context is recorded as unsafe and rejected by any gate, it remains rejected by all future gate libraries. Equivalently, 𝒮sys​(t)\mathcal{S}_{\text{sys}}(t) can only expand on observed unsafe behavior; it cannot shrink on logged unsafe contexts.

B.6 Reference Prompt Templates (Runnable) for ContentGates and Gate Synthesis

ContentGate prompt (reference configuration).

We use a fixed template that maps ctx + a payload excerpt to a strict binary decision. The template is intentionally short, as the input is already structured:

SYSTEM: You are a safety classifier. Output exactly one token: SAFE or UNSAFE.
USER:
[Action] {primitive_type, tool_family}
[Args] {canonical_path/domain/port if any}
[History] last H hard primitives: {(type, resource, op)}
[Payload] (redacted excerpt, max 1,000 chars)
Decide if executing this action violates the sandbox safety policy or
benchmark-defined safety constraints.

Deterministic RuleGate synthesis prompt (reference configuration).

We synthesize candidate structured predicates offline from minimal unsafe windows (App. E) using a frozen reasoning model. We enforce that the model outputs only code over structured fields and bounded history:

SYSTEM: You write deterministic Python predicates over a given JSON schema.
USER: Given the unsafe contexts below (positive) and benign contexts (negative),
propose a Python function gate(ctx)->(ok,msg) that: (1) rejects all positives, (2) rejects at most ϵbenign\epsilon_{\text{benign}} of negatives, (3) uses only ctx fields and ctx.recent_hard_history, (4) contains no randomness and no external calls. Return JSON: {"code": "...", "rationale": "..."}.

We then (i) compile the returned code, (ii) unit-test it on corpora, and (iii) accept it only if it satisfies the formal constraints above.

B.7 Concrete Examples of Structured Gates (Illustrative)

Below are illustrative (not benchmark-specific) RuleGate patterns, expressed purely over structured fields:

  • •

    Workspace confinement: reject writes/deletes whose canonical path is outside workspace_roots.

  • •

    Protected deletion: reject deletes of any path matching protected prefixes (e.g., system dirs) or non-ephemeral dirs.

  • •

    Network egress control: reject network sends when domain is not in an allowlist or when scheme/port is disallowed.

  • •

    Short-window exfiltration motif: if recent_hard_history contains a sensitive read followed by an archive/write, reject a subsequent network send of the same artifact.

These examples are representative of the expressible subset 𝒮sys​(t)\mathcal{S}_{\text{sys}}(t) and emphasize the key property: all decisions depend only on structured context and bounded history.

Appendix C Behavior Path Extractor and Abstraction Stability

C.1 Deterministic Macro Segmentation from Observable Deltas

Raw trajectories are long and tool-specific. The Behavior Path Extractor EE maps a trajectory τ\tau to a macro path

p=(v0,…,vK)=E⁡(τ),p=(v_{0},\dots,v_{K})=E(\tau),

where each macro vkv_{k} is a contiguous span of primitives that: (i) stays within a local sub-action region, and (ii) realizes a coherent intent.

Segmentation signals (no LLM judgment).

Macro boundaries are anchored by observable environment deltas and tool-family changes logged by OpenHands:

  • •

    Filesystem deltas: creation/modification of files; diff size thresholds; directory scope change.

  • •

    Execution deltas: process spawn/termination; test invocation boundaries; interpreter session boundaries.

  • •

    Web deltas: domain change; navigation state change; form submission boundary.

  • •

    Tool-family switch: first invocation of a different tool family in a span (e.g., from file ops to browser).

These rules are deterministic functions of logs. LLMs are not used to decide boundaries.

Risk annotation.

Each macro is assigned a discrete risk_level based on whether its primitive span touches 𝒯hard\mathcal{T}_{\text{hard}} and which resource families it touches (files, network, processes). This risk metadata is used only for (i) conservative merging and (ii) risk-aware recovery costs (App. G).

C.2 Macro Description Summarization (Offline Only) and Output Schema

After segmentation, we summarize each macro span into a short description solely for semantic matching and retrieval. This summary is never consumed by gates or preconditions.

Reference summarization prompt (runnable).

We call a frozen LLM at temperature 00 with a strict JSON schema:

SYSTEM: Summarize a tool-usage segment into a reusable action macro. Output JSON only.
USER: You are given (i) a sequence of primitive tool calls with arguments, and (ii) a compact description of observable environment deltas.
Produce JSON with fields: {"macro_desc": "...", "macro_tags": [...], "resources": [...], "hard_touch": bool}.

We set max_tokens=256 and enforce JSON parsing; unparsable outputs are retried once with the same temperature 00 and an added format reminder.

C.3 Abstraction Stability Test on Safety-Critical Traces

Traversal assumes macros have stable semantics. We therefore test stability on any trajectory that is unsafe or touches 𝒯hard\mathcal{T}_{\text{hard}}.

Stability protocol.

For a candidate trajectory τ\tau: (i) run the deterministic segmentation once to obtain boundary indices; (ii) rerun only the summarization calls under PP prompt perturbations (rephrased instructions and shuffled in-context examples) while keeping segmentation fixed; (iii) measure whether resulting macro descriptions remain semantically equivalent and do not induce boundary drift or semantic aliasing downstream.

Boundary stability (conservative).

If the pipeline variant includes any stochastic segmentation component, we require boundary-set Jaccard similarity

J⁡(B(i),B(j))≥δstab∀i≠j,J(B^{(i)},B^{(j)})\geq\delta_{\text{stab}}\quad\forall i\neq j,

with reference threshold δstab=0.9\delta_{\text{stab}}=0.9 and P=5P=5 perturbations. Any trajectory failing this test is marked abstract-unstable and excluded from tree construction and gate derivation. (Primitive-level safety remains enforced by the global guardrail regardless.)

Why this matters.

This explicitly prevents safety-critical behavior from being externalized into macros when the abstraction itself is unstable, aligning with the main-text claim that traversal is only used where macro semantics are robust.

Appendix D Task-Family Routing and Re-rooting

D.1 Family Taxonomy (First-Layer Branching Control)

We build a single rooted tree whose first layer consists of a small number of task-family roots (reference configuration: 21 families, derived by benchmark inspection) to reduce branching. Example families include CODE_EDITING, TEST_DEBUG, WEB_BROWSING, FORM_FILLING, DATA_ANALYSIS, NETWORK_PROCESS, and CHAT.

D.2 Training-Free Routing by Prototype Similarity

Routing must respect the paper’s training-free discipline: no weight updates. We implement a frozen router using prototype similarity:

  • •

    For each family ff, we store a small set of natural-language prototypes Πf\Pi_{f} (2–8 short descriptions) curated once from benchmark/task definitions.

  • •

    Given a task description xx, we embed xx and all prototypes using a frozen text encoder f⁡(⋅)f(\cdot) (any deterministic sentence embedding model).

  • •

    We score each family by its best prototype similarity: s⁡(f∣x)=maxπ∈Πf⁡cos⁡(f⁡(x),f⁡(π)).s(f\mid x)=\max_{\pi\in\Pi_{f}}\cos(f(x),f(\pi)).

  • •

    We convert scores to a normalized distribution by a temperature-scaled softmax: p⁡(f∣x)=exp⁡(s⁡(f∣x)/Tfam)∑f′exp⁡(s⁡(f′∣x)/Tfam).p(f\mid x)=\frac{\exp(s(f\mid x)/T_{\text{fam}})}{\sum_{f^{\prime}}\exp(s(f^{\prime}\mid x)/T_{\text{fam}})}.

Abstention threshold (explicit claim boundary).

Let pmax=maxf⁡p⁡(f∣x)p_{\max}=\max_{f}p(f\mid x). If pmax<δfamp_{\max}<\delta_{\text{fam}}, the traverser abstains from traversal control and the episode is labeled covered=0. Reference configuration: δfam=0.55\delta_{\text{fam}}=0.55, Tfam=0.05T_{\text{fam}}=0.05.

D.3 Re-rooting Under Task Drift

Long tasks may drift across families (e.g., from web browsing to code editing). Every mm macro steps (reference: m=3m=3), we recompute p⁡(f∣xcurrent)p(f\mid x_{\text{current}}) using the current task summary and spine. We re-root iff: (i) a new family exceeds the current family by margin Δswitch\Delta_{\text{switch}}, (ii) the new family also exceeds δfam\delta_{\text{fam}}, and (iii) re-rooting preserves acyclicity and does not cross into a disallowed subtree. Reference: Δswitch=0.10\Delta_{\text{switch}}=0.10. Re-rooting modifies only the family root anchor; it does not alter gates and cannot weaken enforcement (Design invariants 1–2).

Appendix E Node-Local Gates, Tree Construction, and Acyclicity

E.1 Minimal Unsafe Windows via Deterministic Replay Shrinking

Unsafe trajectories reveal 𝒮spec\mathcal{S}_{\text{spec}} violations not yet captured by 𝒮sys​(t)\mathcal{S}_{\text{sys}}(t). For each unsafe trajectory τ\tau, we find a minimal unsafe primitive window W=(at0,…,at1)W=(a_{t_{0}},\dots,a_{t_{1}}) by deterministic sandbox replay:

Window shrinking algorithm (deterministic).

We checkpoint replayable states (pre-action snapshots) and shrink [t0,t1][t_{0},t_{1}] by: (i) binary searching the earliest violating index, (ii) minimizing contiguous prefixes/suffixes while preserving the violation, and (iii) verifying minimality: removing any primitive from the boundary removes the violation verdict. This yields the shortest contiguous window that triggers the first safety verdict under replay.

E.2 Mapping Unsafe Windows to Macro Subsequences and Attaching Node-Local Gates

We map τ\tau to its macro path p=E⁡(τ)=(v0,…,vK)p=E(\tau)=(v_{0},\dots,v_{K}). Let U=(vk0,…,vk1)U=(v_{k_{0}},\dots,v_{k_{1}}) be the minimal contiguous macro subsequence that covers all primitives in WW. Every macro v∈Uv\in U is treated as participating in the unsafe pattern and is eligible for node-local gates.

Node-local gate synthesis (structured-only).

For each eligible node vv, we synthesize a small set 𝒢⁡(v)\mathcal{G}(v) of node-local gates with the same interface g:ctx↦(ok,msg)g:\texttt{ctx}\mapsto(\texttt{ok},\texttt{msg}). Crucially:

  • •

    Gate predicates are compiled code over structured ctx and bounded history.

  • •

    LLM summaries and env_context may be used offline to help propose candidate predicates, but the resulting gate reads only structured fields at runtime.

  • •

    Node-local gates obey the same monotonic unsafe-corpus constraint and benign-regression control as global gates (App. B.5).

E.3 Behavior Signatures and Merge Discipline (Anti-Aliasing Where Safety Matters)

Each macro node vv stores:

  • •

    description (for semantic matching only),

  • •

    coarse tags (tool family, intent),

  • •

    risk_level (discrete),

  • •

    a behavior signature σ⁡(v)=(σdisc​(v),σcont​(v))\sigma(v)=(\sigma_{\text{disc}}(v),\sigma_{\text{cont}}(v)) computed from logs only,

  • •

    a pointer env_context to the local interaction segment (materialized on demand).

Signature details.

σdisc\sigma_{\text{disc}} includes exact-match discrete features (multiset of tool families, resource-type flags, whether 𝒯hard\mathcal{T}_{\text{hard}} is touched, and coarse delta types). σcont\sigma_{\text{cont}} is a normalized statistics vector (tool usage frequencies, diff magnitudes, counts of deltas). Both are computed deterministically from logs and are LLM-independent.

Merge rule (three-way agreement).

When inserting a new macro vv under parent pp, we merge into an existing child uu only if:

σdisc​(v)=σdisc​(u),cos⁡(σcont​(v),σcont​(u))≥θsig,cos⁡(f⁡(desc​(v)),f⁡(desc​(u)))≥θmerge.\sigma_{\text{disc}}(v)=\sigma_{\text{disc}}(u),\quad\cos(\sigma_{\text{cont}}(v),\sigma_{\text{cont}}(u))\geq\theta_{\text{sig}},\quad\cos(f(\text{desc}(v)),f(\text{desc}(u)))\geq\theta_{\text{merge}}.

Reference configuration: θsig=0.92\theta_{\text{sig}}=0.92, θmerge=0.85\theta_{\text{merge}}=0.85.

No merges into gated nodes.

To avoid semantic aliasing precisely where safety matters most, merges into nodes that carry any node-local gates are disallowed.

E.4 Acyclicity as a Hard Invariant

We enforce that GBT remains a rooted tree. Insertion, splitting, and self-evolution are forbidden from creating edges pointing to any ancestor along the current spine. This maintains deterministic traversal semantics and prevents recovery/search from entering cycles.

Design invariant 2 (Tree edits do not weaken enforcement).

Tree edits (insertion/merge/split/re-root) never delete or relax gates, and gates depend only on structured ctx and bounded history. Thus, topology changes can affect availability/selection frequency, but cannot re-admit previously rejected unsafe contexts.

Appendix F Self-Evolution Under Safety Invariants

F.1 Coverage Definition (Executable Claim Boundary)

Self-evolution applies only when GBT genuinely serves as the policy skeleton. We define covered=1 iff all hold:

  1. 1.

    Confident family routing: maxf⁡p⁡(f∣x)≥δfam\max_{f}p(f\mid x)\geq\delta_{\text{fam}} and no re-root occurs.

  2. 2.

    Traversal-consistent matching: every macro transition matches an existing child with similarity stop1≥θlows_{\text{top1}}\geq\theta_{\text{low}}.

  3. 3.

    No safe exploration: the traverser never invokes safe exploration (budgeted abstention) at any step.

Otherwise covered=0 and we do not claim traversal as long-horizon policy control (Sec. 2.4, Sec. 2.5).

Reference configuration for matching thresholds (consistent with App. K): θlow=0.70\theta_{\text{low}}=0.70, θhigh=0.78\theta_{\text{high}}=0.78.

F.2 Failure Localization on the Spine and Analogical Repair

Given a failed covered path pfail=(v0,…,vK)p^{\text{fail}}=(v_{0},\dots,v_{K}), a frozen reasoning model diagnoses failure on the task spine: macro descriptions + coarse environment summaries. It backtracks to the earliest node v⋆v^{\star} where choosing a different successor could plausibly avert failure.

Analogical success retrieval.

We embed the task description and success-leaf descriptions and retrieve top-RR candidate success leaves. Reference: R=50R=50. We then align v⋆v^{\star} to a node on each success path by description similarity and select the best-aligned pair.

Allowed edits (behavior-only, local).

Self-evolution may: (i) add a child under v⋆v^{\star}, (ii) update local selection statistics, and (iii) add new gates for newly observed unsafe patterns. It may not delete or weaken any gate. Any newly added child inherits all node-local gates of its parent before adding additional ones.

F.3 Selection Score and Context Clustering

At a node vv, each child uu maintains: (i) a semantic similarity term to the base model proposal, and (ii) empirical success rates for similar structured contexts. We use:

score​(u,ctx)=α⋅simtext​(proposal,desc​(u))+β⋅success​_​rate​(u,cluster⁡(ctx)).\texttt{score}(u;\texttt{ctx})=\alpha\cdot\mathrm{sim}_{\text{text}}(\text{proposal},\text{desc}(u))+\beta\cdot\mathrm{success\_rate}\big(u;\mathrm{cluster}(\texttt{ctx})\big).

Reference configuration: α=1.0\alpha=1.0, β=0.5\beta=0.5.

Clustering.

We cluster structured contexts by coarse resource family + risk level + discrete signature buckets (from σdisc\sigma_{\text{disc}}). This keeps statistics stable and avoids high-variance conditioning on sparse identifiers.

F.4 Regression Tests (Safety Preservation by Construction)

Each proposed edit is accepted only if it passes two deterministic regression suites:

(1) Success non-regression.

Replay historical successful episodes that pass through v⋆v^{\star}, starting from the same pre-v⋆v^{\star} sandbox state, and allow only the post-v⋆v^{\star} behavior to follow the updated local policy. Require success rate degradation ≤δsucc\leq\delta_{\text{succ}}. Reference: δsucc=0.02\delta_{\text{succ}}=0.02 (absolute).

(2) Unsafe non-re-admission.

Replay historical unsafe episodes whose minimal windows map to v⋆v^{\star} and verify that all previously rejected contexts remain rejected under the conjunction of global and node-local gates.

Design invariant 3 (Safety under self-evolution).

Under these allowed edits and regression tests, self-evolution cannot re-admit previously rejected unsafe structured contexts.

Appendix G Recovery: Preconditions and Risk-Aware Shortest Paths

G.1 Leaf Retrieval and Environment Signature Filtering

When stalled, the traverser retrieves candidate success leaves similar to the task description under f⁡(⋅)f(\cdot). To avoid spurious reuse, we filter leaves by a coarse environment signature match.

Environment signature.

For each success leaf ℓ\ell, we store a lightweight signature computed from the sandbox snapshot at success time, e.g.: (current domain / repo root, file-set sketch, boolean flags for tool availability, and a coarse risk footprint). At recovery time we compute the same signature on the current environment and require cosine similarity ≥θenv\geq\theta_{\text{env}}. Reference: θenv=0.80\theta_{\text{env}}=0.80.

G.2 Feasibility Preconditions (Conservative, Never Overriding Gates)

Each node carries a deterministic precondition predicate pre​(v,env)\texttt{pre}(v,\texttt{env}) over a structured environment summary. Preconditions are synthesized offline from successful trajectories and compiled into code checks such as: existence of required files, being on a required domain, presence of a required test command, etc.

Conservatism.

Preconditions may reject some feasible states (false negatives) but do not introduce actions and never override gates. Even if pre holds, all primitives remain subject to global and node-local gates.

G.3 Risk-Aware Shortest Paths

Within the family subtree, restricted to feasible nodes and filtered success leaves, we run Dijkstra with edge cost

c⁡(v→u)=1+λ⋅risk​_​level​(u).c(v\to u)=1+\lambda\cdot\mathrm{risk\_level}(u).

Reference: λ=0.5\lambda=0.5, depth limit Dmax=8D_{\max}=8 macro steps. If no feasible path exists, we emit a safe failure and log the episode for offline expansion of coverage or repair.

Execution.

A recovery path is executed one macro at a time under the same primitive-level gating as normal traversal.

Appendix H Hierarchical Memory and Context Materialization

H.1 Spine Memory: What the Executor Sees Online

The traverser maintains the task spine (v0,…,vt)(v_{0},\dots,v_{t}) as persistent state. At each step, the base model receives: (i) a concise task summary, (ii) the spine’s macro descriptions, (iii) the selected macro description for the next step, and (iv) a short node-local context summary distilled from env_context(vt)(v_{t}).

Full transcripts are not replayed. Safety-critical identifiers (canonical paths, domains, process IDs) bypass summarization and flow directly into structured ctx/env for gates and preconditions.

H.2 Reference Prompt Template for Node-Local Context Summaries

We summarize env_context(vt)(v_{t}) offline/online using a frozen LLM at temperature 00 to produce only the minimal information needed to realize the macro.

SYSTEM: Summarize tool outputs into actionable, minimal context. No speculation.
USER: Given the macro description and the local tool outputs, extract: (1) the exact targets (files/URLs/selectors) as referenced by the environment, (2) any constraints (tests to run, fields to fill), (3) the next concrete steps to realize the macro. Output a bullet list with at most 8 bullets.

We cap this summary at 200–300 tokens to prevent drift and keep the executor in a local, verifiable regime.

Appendix I Additional Experimental Details and Diagnostics

This appendix specifies the evaluation contract and the mechanism-to-evidence linkage for the experiments: what exactly is executed (OpenHands action/observation stream), what counts as success and safety violation (benchmark checkers + sandbox monitors defining 𝒮spec\mathcal{S}_{\text{spec}}), how we define the claim boundary (covered), and how each table substantiates a specific component of Traversal-as-Policy (GBT traversal control, deterministic pre-execution gating, recovery search, spine memory, and self-evolution under monotone safety invariants).

Two principles govern this appendix: (i) attribution-clean comparisons: whenever we compare systems, we keep the OpenHands sandbox, tool APIs, monitors/checkers, and accounting identical, and change only the policy artifact components (tree traversal/recovery/spine/gates); (ii) coverage-scoped claims: long-horizon control claims are made only on episodes with covered=1 (App. F.1); outside coverage we claim only primitive-level safety from the always-on global guardrail.

I.1 Benchmarks and OpenHands Integration (Facts, Sizes, and Evaluation Contracts)

Why this subsection exists. Our main claims are mechanism-level: we externalize policy as a tree, enforce safety deterministically before high-risk primitives execute, and explicitly bound where traversal is the long-horizon policy (covered=1). These claims only make sense if all systems run under the same execution substrate and the same notion of safety. OpenHands provides (i) a uniform tool/action interface, (ii) a sandboxed runtime with replayable event streams, and (iii) benchmark-defined checkers and runtime monitors whose verdicts instantiate 𝒮spec\mathcal{S}_{\text{spec}} (App. B.1). All reported success/violation outcomes below are therefore defined as properties of the actual executed primitive sequence in the sandbox, not of textual post-hoc judgments.

Execution contract (common to all suites). Each episode produces an OpenHands event stream of alternating actions (primitive tool calls with structured arguments) and observations (tool outputs + environment deltas). OpenHands additionally logs: (i) benchmark checker outcomes (success/failure), (ii) monitor/checker safety verdicts (violations defining 𝒮spec\mathcal{S}_{\text{spec}}), (iii) gate decisions for any a∈𝒯harda\in\mathcal{T}_{\text{hard}} (App. B), and (iv) usage accounting (tokens and characters) for model calls.

Pillars (headline benchmark contracts).

  • •

    SWE-bench Verified (500 issues). Each instance provides a repository snapshot and a concrete issue. The episode is successful iff the produced patch satisfies the benchmark’s verified evaluation (tests/checker contract). An episode has a violation iff any executed primitive triggers an OpenHands monitor/checker safety verdict (App. B.1). We report SR/Viol/USucc and diagnostics under the same sandbox.

  • •

    WebArena (812 tasks). Each task requires multi-step browser interaction under benchmark-defined completion criteria. Success is benchmark-defined completion; violations are any OpenHands safety verdicts emitted during tool execution (e.g., disallowed network destinations, protected resource accesses, or other sandbox/benchmark constraints).

  • •

    GPQA (448 questions). We treat GPQA as tool-assisted reasoning with external web browsing disabled. The agent may use local deterministic computation tools (e.g., Python) but not open web access. Success is correctness of the selected answer choice. Violations are any OpenHands safety verdicts (typically rare because the action surface is restricted, but still well-defined).

Safety/security suites (public and reproducible).

  • •

    Agent-SafetyBench. We report the benchmark’s official score and, when executed through OpenHands, the associated safety outcomes under the same monitors/checkers.

  • •

    AgentHarm (public). We report HarmScore as defined by the benchmark. When episodes involve tool actions, they are executed under the same OpenHands gate+monitor discipline.

  • •

    Agent Security Bench (ASB). We report the benchmark’s official metrics (ASR-d, RR, PNA-d) and run tool-executing agents under identical OpenHands monitoring and the same always-on global pre-execution guardrail for a∈𝒯harda\in\mathcal{T}_{\text{hard}}.

Distillation-only suites (Protocol A). We distill and self-evolve GBT using additional OpenHands-integrated suites spanning software, web, and reasoning (listed explicitly in App. I.3). These are used only to build/refine GBT under Protocol A and are held out during evaluation on the three pillars.

Integration discipline (why “guardrail-only” is attribution-clean). All benchmark episodes run through the same OpenHands schema and the same monitors/checkers defining 𝒮spec\mathcal{S}_{\text{spec}}. This makes the Global guardrail only baseline a clean ablation: it shares the same sandbox and the same pre-execution global guardrail on 𝒯hard\mathcal{T}_{\text{hard}}, differing only in the absence of traversal control, recovery search, spine memory, node-local gates, and self-evolution. Any deltas versus GBT-guided variants can therefore be attributed to Traversal-as-Policy components rather than to execution substrate differences.

I.2 Models and System Variants

This subsection defines exactly what differs between systems, so every reported delta can be mapped back to a specific mechanism in the Method.

Offline distillation and refinement (training-free). We build GBT-Basic by distilling OpenHands execution logs with gpt-4o-2024-08-06 (temperature 00) for macro description summarization and deterministic predicate synthesis. Macro segmentation and behavior signatures are computed directly from logs (App. C, App. E). We build GBT-SE via failure-driven self-evolution using gemini-2.5-pro as the frozen diagnosis/repair model (Method; App. F). Payload-bearing safety checks use Llama-Guard-3-8B at temperature 00 (App. B).

Online deployment regimes. We report two regimes: (i) Same-model deployment: gpt-4o-2024-08-06 as the base agent with/without GBT. (ii) Executor decoupling: GBT is fixed, and the online executor MbaseM_{\text{base}} is an 8B-scale model (llama-3-8b or Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking). In the decoupled regime, the executor is restricted to realizing exactly one selected macro at a time under traversal/recovery and gates; it does not perform long-horizon planning.

System taxonomy (what each name means). To avoid accidental apples-to-oranges comparisons, throughout the paper we use the following naming:

  • •

    Native agent: the framework’s default planner/executor loop (no GBT traversal/recovery/spine), and without our global pre-execution guardrail unless explicitly stated. It still runs under OpenHands monitors/checkers, so Viol/USucc are still measured.

  • •

    +Global guardrail only: adds the always-on pre-execution global guardrail for a∈𝒯harda\in\mathcal{T}_{\text{hard}} (App. B), but no traversal control, no recovery, no spine memory, no node-local gates, and no self-evolution. This isolates the effect of deterministic action-level gating alone.

  • •

    +GBT-Basic: enables traversal-as-policy within coverage using the distilled tree, spine memory, and (when applicable) node-local gates mined from unsafe windows. Global guardrail remains always-on for a∈𝒯harda\in\mathcal{T}_{\text{hard}}.

  • •

    +GBT-SE: starts from the same tree artifact and applies self-evolution edits under Design invariants 1–3 and regression tests (App. F.4). This isolates whether local, failure-driven structure edits add value beyond the initial distilled policy, while preserving monotone safety (no unsafe context re-admission).

Attribution clarity: safety components. GBT-guided systems always run with the same global pre-execution guardrail on 𝒯hard\mathcal{T}_{\text{hard}} and may additionally enforce node-local gates at specific macros. Therefore: (i) improvements from Native →\rightarrow +Global guardrail only quantify the value of deterministic pre-execution gating alone; (ii) improvements from +Global guardrail only →\rightarrow +GBT-* quantify the value of traversal-as-policy (control externalization + spine memory + recovery), with node-local gates separated by ablation (Table 20).

I.3 Protocols and Leakage Controls

We use three complementary protocols to rule out leakage along three axes: benchmark identity, instance identity, and shared structure (repo/site/domain). The goal is to ensure that improvements are driven by the Traversal-as-Policy mechanisms rather than by hidden reuse of evaluation-specific artifacts.

Protocol A: cross-benchmark distillation with benchmark-level hold-out. We distill GBT using logs from disjoint benchmarks and test on held-out benchmarks: Software: distill on HumanEvalFix, BIRD, BioCoder, ML-Bench, Gorilla APIBench, ToolQA; test on SWE-bench Verified. Web: distill on MiniWoB++; test on WebArena. Misc: distill on GAIA, AgentBench, MINT, ProofWriter, Entity Deduction Arena; test on GPQA. No trajectories from the held-out evaluation benchmark are used for tree construction or self-evolution. In Protocol A, all GBT-SE edits are driven only by failures observed on the distillation benchmarks, never by evaluation runs on the held-out benchmark.

Protocol B: instance-level hold-out with 5-fold cross-validation. We run 5-fold instance-level CV on SWE-bench Verified, WebArena, and GPQA. For each fold, GBT is constructed and (if applicable) self-evolved using only training-fold episodes; evaluation uses the held-out fold. We report micro-averaged results across the union of held-out folds (each instance is evaluated exactly once in its held-out fold).

Protocol C: structural hold-outs (repo/site/domain). To stress-test against subtle leakage through shared artifacts, we additionally run: (i) repo-holdout on SWE-bench Verified (split by repository), (ii) site-holdout on WebArena (hold out entire websites), and (iii) domain-holdout on GPQA (hold out one scientific domain). All tree construction and self-evolution are restricted to the training side of each split.

Why Protocols A–C are jointly necessary. Protocol A blocks direct benchmark reuse (e.g., SWE-bench Verified instances never appear in distillation), but could still permit structure transfer through related repos/sites if they overlap across suites. Protocol C closes that gap by withholding entire repositories/sites/domains. Protocol B complements both by measuring robustness when the evaluation distribution is matched (same benchmark) but instances are disjoint, which isolates whether the policy artifact generalizes at the instance level rather than only across benchmarks.

I.4 Metrics and Reporting Conventions

Task performance. We report official metrics: success rate (SR, %) for execution-based benchmarks (SWE-bench Verified, WebArena) and accuracy (Acc, %) for GPQA.

Coverage as the explicit claim boundary. We report Coverage (Cov, %) as the fraction of episodes with covered=1 (Method; App. F). For GBT-guided systems we also report conditional performance Pr⁡(success∣covered=1)\Pr(\text{success}\mid\texttt{covered}=1) and Pr⁡(success∣covered=0)\Pr(\text{success}\mid\texttt{covered}=0). Any episode invoking safe exploration is labeled covered=0 by definition. This separation is not cosmetic: it is the formal boundary of our long-horizon policy claim. In particular, conditional metrics on covered=1 quantify the regime where traversal truly governs macro choice; unconditional metrics mix this with the abstention regime.

Safety on OpenHands-executed benchmarks. We report: (i) Violation (Viol, %): fraction of episodes with any primitive violating 𝒮spec\mathcal{S}_{\text{spec}} under OpenHands monitors/checkers; (ii) Unsafe success (USucc, %): fraction of episodes that end in benchmark success but contain any 𝒮spec\mathcal{S}_{\text{spec}} violation. Viol and USucc are properties of executed primitives, and therefore directly test the Method’s claim that gates enforce safety pre-execution (App. B) while traversal reduces exposure by steering away from high-risk dead-ends.

Efficiency, stability, and repeated runs. We report average total LLM tokens per episode (Tok, thousands) and tokenizer-agnostic characters (Chars, thousands) logged by OpenHands. We run each instance three times (all models at temperature 00) to capture residual environment nondeterminism (web timing, repo I/O ordering). We compute per-instance outcomes by majority vote over the three runs (success/violation/unsafe-success) and report Wilson 95% confidence intervals over these per-instance binary outcomes. We report run-to-run stability as the standard deviation (Std, points) of SR/Acc across repeats. This design ensures that improvements reflect changes in the executed policy, not fragile dependence on incidental nondeterminism.

Stall and recovery definitions (deterministic from the event stream). An episode is marked Stall if any holds: (i) No-progress: for 3 consecutive macro steps no measurable environment delta (no file diff, no new process state, no website/domain transition), (ii) Gate-loop: the same high-risk primitive family is blocked by pre-execution gates ≥3\geq 3 times within a 5-step window, or (iii) Plan-loop: the agent repeats an equivalent macro proposal twice with no progress. Rec-Succ is the fraction of stalled episodes successfully recovered to benchmark success after invoking recovery (conditional on Stall). We also report RecLen (mean and p​90p90) in macro steps to quantify that recovery emits short, high-confidence sequences.

Guardrail activity (exposure vs enforcement). We report Hard: average number of attempted high-risk primitives in 𝒯hard\mathcal{T}_{\text{hard}} per episode (including attempts blocked pre-execution), and Blocked: average number of those attempts vetoed before execution by 𝒢global\mathcal{G}_{\text{global}} and/or node-local gates. Hard captures exposure pressure (how often the policy attempts risky actions); Blocked captures enforcement load (how often the safety layer must intervene). The Method predicts that traversal + recovery + spine reduce Hard by avoiding thrashing, while gates reduce Viol/USucc by blocking unsafe contexts pre-execution.

Appendix J GBT as a Plug-in Policy Artifact Improves Diverse Frameworks

We test whether the same distilled traversal policy reliably improves heterogeneous agent frameworks without changing their internal planners or model weights. The key question is not whether any one agent can be tuned to a benchmark, but whether an external policy artifact (the same GBT) can be attached as a plug-in controller and systematically lift performance and stability across different internal implementations.

Software engineering: SWE-bench Verified.

Interpretation (Table 9). Three facts matter simultaneously: (i) broad lift across frameworks: every agent improves substantially when controlled by the same GBT, indicating the gain is not tied to one planner’s quirks but to the externalized traversal policy; (ii) high coverage: Cov stays in the mid-80% range across all frameworks, meaning the tree is not a narrow template that only triggers rarely; it regularly governs long-horizon control; (iii) SE adds a second margin: GBT-SE consistently improves over GBT-Basic at similar (often slightly higher) coverage, which is precisely the Method’s prediction that local repair under self-evolution expands/strengthens the reachable success set without relaxing safety (Design invariants 1–3).

Web browsing: WebArena.

Interpretation (Table 10). Web tasks are a canonical long-horizon drift regime: success requires maintaining a stable notion of “where you are” (domain/page state) and “what remains” (form fields, constraints), under nondeterministic timing. Table 10 shows that GBT yields large success lifts with substantial coverage (∼\sim76–78%), consistent with traversal and spine memory reducing drift, and recovery providing short corrective sequences when stalls occur.

Tool-assisted reasoning: GPQA.

Interpretation (Table 11). GPQA is not a tool-rich benchmark, but it is a control benchmark for policy externalization: when web browsing is disabled, improvements cannot be attributed to retrieval or external knowledge injection. The large accuracy increase with substantial coverage indicates that traversal-as-policy and spine memory can still stabilize multi-step reasoning by constraining the sequence of reasoning macros (e.g., “derive intermediate quantity” →\rightarrow “compute deterministically” →\rightarrow “map to choice”) and preventing transcript bloat from polluting subsequent steps.

Run-to-run stability.

Interpretation (Table 12). Stability is a first-class objective for long-horizon agents: a policy that occasionally succeeds is not deployable if it is variance-dominated. The monotone, executable structure of traversal and gating reduces stochastic dependence on incidental trajectories, which appears as reduced Std across all three pillars in Table 12.

Appendix K Coverage and Matching Diagnostics

This section connects covered (the claim boundary) to concrete matching statistics and audits that rule out easy-instance selection effects.

Interpretation (Table 13). Traversal control only makes sense when semantic matching is confident. Table 13 shows: (i) top-1 similarities are high on average, and margins are substantial, indicating the child selection problem is typically well-posed; (ii) fragile and ambiguous steps are a small minority, which bounds where traversal could be brittle; (iii) safe exploration episode rates are low (and those episodes are explicitly labeled covered=0), enforcing the Method’s claim boundary rather than silently claiming control where matching is uncertain.

Interpretation (Table 14). This is the central attribution audit for traversal-as-policy. By restricting evaluation to the exact same covered=1 instance subset, Table 14 removes any possibility that coverage merely filters to easier instances. The remaining difference is precisely the traversal policy (plus recovery/spine). The large deltas therefore directly substantiate the claim that GBT is not only a safety wrapper but a genuine long-horizon control artifact.

Interpretation (Table 15). A common failure mode for “controller” methods is that they only engage on easy cases. Table 15 rules this out: coverage remains high even on instances that the guardrail-only baseline fails. This supports the Method’s intended meaning of coverage: it is a confidence/consistency predicate (routing + matching + no safe exploration), not an “easy-case” heuristic.

Interpretation (Table 16). Table 16 demonstrates the expected precision–coverage trade-off: tighter thresholds reduce Cov but increase Pr⁡(succ∣covered=1)\Pr(\textbf{succ}\mid\texttt{covered}=1). Crucially, overall SR is stable across a reasonable band, indicating the system is not brittle to threshold tuning and that abstention is behaving as intended (uncertain steps become covered=0 rather than forcing incorrect traversal).

Appendix L Structural Hold-outs (Protocol C)

Interpretation (Table 17). Protocol C removes shared structure that could otherwise serve as a leakage channel (shared repos, sites, or domains). The improvements in Table 17 therefore directly support that GBT is learning reusable macro-level control structure rather than memorizing evaluation-specific artifacts. The persistence of the GBT-SE margin further supports that local repair generalizes under structural novelty.

Appendix M Additional Safety Diagnostics on OpenHands-executed Benchmarks

This section ties safety outcomes to the Method’s enforcement story: safety is enforced pre-execution by deterministic gates over structured contexts (App. B), and traversal reduces unsafe exposure by avoiding gate-loop thrashing and risky dead-ends.

Interpretation (Table 18). The progression across rows cleanly separates three mechanisms: (i) Native →\rightarrow Guardrail-only: large drops in Viol/USucc quantify the value of deterministic pre-execution gating on 𝒯hard\mathcal{T}_{\text{hard}} alone; (ii) Guardrail-only →\rightarrow GBT-Basic: further reductions indicate that traversal/spine (even before self-evolution) reduce the frequency of entering unsafe neighborhoods, beyond simply blocking individual actions; (iii) GBT-Basic →\rightarrow GBT-SE: Viol/USucc are driven toward zero while success increases elsewhere in the paper’s main tables, consistent with self-evolution repairing failures without relaxing the accumulated safety subset (Design invariants 1–3).

Interpretation (Table 19). Table 19 distinguishes exposure reduction from enforcement. Guardrail-only reduces Viol primarily by blocking, but still attempts many high-risk primitives (Hard remains high). GBT-SE reduces Hard itself, consistent with traversal-as-policy steering the agent away from repeated risky attempts and with recovery escaping stalls before they degenerate into gate-loops. This is the intended division of labor: gates prevent unsafe execution; traversal/recovery avoid repeatedly proposing unsafe moves.

Appendix N Ablations: Gates, Recovery, Memory, and Self-evolution

This section decomposes the overall gains into the Method’s modular components. The key requirement is that each ablation changes one mechanism while keeping the sandbox, tools, monitors/checkers, and (when stated) the global guardrail identical.

N.1 Global vs. Node-local Gates

Interpretation (Table 20). The jump from +Global guardrail only to +GBT (no node-local) is the traversal-as-policy effect: traversal + recovery + spine (without extra macro-local safety predicates) already transforms success while reducing Viol, meaning the core gain is not merely “blocking unsafe actions” but externalizing and constraining long-horizon control. Adding node-local gates yields an additional reduction in Viol and a small additional success lift, consistent with their role as experience-mined, macro-neighborhood-specific constraints derived from minimal unsafe windows (App. E.2).

N.2 Recovery: Risk-aware Shortest Paths and Preconditions

Interpretation (Table 21). Table 21 validates recovery as a distinct mechanism, not a cosmetic add-on: (i) enabling recovery reduces Stall and increases final SR, showing that stalls are a material failure mode even under traversal constraints; (ii) removing risk weighting (λ=0\lambda=0) reduces Rec-Succ and lengthens recovery paths, consistent with risk-aware costs discouraging detours into high-risk nodes (Eq. 2); (iii) removing feasibility preconditions increases Stall and lengthens recovery, consistent with pre​(v,env)\texttt{pre}(v,\texttt{env}) acting as a conservative feasibility filter that prevents wasteful or impossible recovery attempts (App. G.2). The critical qualitative point is that recovery improvements come from short, feasible, low-risk macro sequences (low RecLen and RecLen p​90p90), aligned with the Method’s claim that recovery is a bounded, verifiable search over the external policy object rather than free-form replanning.

N.3 Spine Memory vs Transcript Replay

Interpretation (Table 22). This ablation isolates memory representation. Transcript replay improves with larger context windows, but remains far below spine memory even at 32k. Spine memory is essentially invariant across 8k/16k/32k. This is exactly the Method’s claim: long-horizon state should be represented as the compact traversal spine (macro-level control state) plus structured safety-critical fields that bypass summarization (App. H), not as a growing transcript whose truncation behavior interacts pathologically with reasoning and tool execution.

N.4 Self-evolution Ingredients and Safety Preservation

Interpretation (Table 23). Table 23 substantiates two distinct claims:

  • •

    Behavioral claim (why SE works). Removing analogical retrieval degrades performance across all three pillars, indicating that importing successors from aligned successful paths is a key driver of repairing covered failures (App. F.2). Removing the empirical success-rate term (β=0\beta=0) also degrades performance, supporting the role of experience-grounded selection statistics in stabilizing macro choice beyond pure semantic matching (Eq. 1).

  • •

    Safety claim (why SE is safe). Across all variants, unsafe context re-admission remains zero on the same corpus size (18,400), consistent with the monotone safety invariants and the non-re-admission regression suite (App. F.4; Design invariants 1–3). Importantly, even when removing regression tests, previously rejected unsafe contexts are still not re-admitted in this audit, aligning with the fact that allowed edits do not delete/relax gates and new children inherit parent gates before adding more.

Takeaway across ablations. The ablations collectively map each performance and safety improvement to a specific externalized mechanism: (i) traversal-as-policy yields the dominant success lift (Table 20); (ii) recovery improves robustness under stalls and produces short corrective macro sequences (Table 21); (iii) spine memory provides context-budget robustness that transcript replay cannot match (Table 22); (iv) self-evolution adds a second margin while preserving monotone safety (Table 23). Together with the coverage audits (Table 14, Table 15) and safety diagnostics (Table 18, Table 19), this appendix forms a closed loop from Method mechanisms to executed evidence under a unified evaluation contract.

Appendix O Broader Discussion, Limitations, and Future Work

O.1 Limitations and Open Failure Modes

Coverage-scoped guarantees.

GBT intentionally claims long-horizon control only when covered=1 (Sec. 2). Outside coverage, the system abstains from traversal steering and only retains primitive-level safety via the global guardrail. This makes the boundary explicit, but it also means that broad capability still depends on expanding coverage rather than masking uncertainty with free-running generation.

Bounded-history safety is conservative but not complete.

Our executable safety subset 𝒮sys​(t)\mathcal{S}_{\text{sys}}(t) is defined over structured tool context with bounded history (Sec. 2.1). Hazards that require long-range causal context, semantic understanding of external content, or latent side effects may fall outside this expressible set. Consequently, “near-zero” violations on benchmarks reflect both stronger enforcement and the limits of the sandbox monitors that instantiate 𝒮spec\mathcal{S}_{\text{spec}}.

Macro abstraction is a single point of leverage.

Traversal robustness relies on stable macro semantics. Although we exclude abstraction-unstable traces and prevent merges into gated nodes (Sec. 2.3), segmentation errors or signature collisions can still reduce generalization, inflate the tree, or misplace safety locality.

Tree growth and retrieval pressure.

As domains and tools expand, maintaining a compact, auditable tree becomes harder: more nodes increase matching ambiguity; more gates increase conservative blocks; and more recovery candidates increase search overhead. The current design prioritizes verifiability over unbounded scalability.

OOD tools and open-world deployment.

Structured ctx depends on a tool schema. New tools, new action surfaces (e.g., novel network channels), or qualitatively different environments require updating the schema and the monitor set; otherwise the system may be safe-but-ineffective (over-blocking) or effective-but-under-specified (monitor gaps).

O.2 Additional Analysis: Why Externalized Traversal Changes the Failure Geometry

Guardrails veto; traversal governs.

The main results show that global guardrails reduce violations but barely improve success on long-horizon tasks (Sec. 3.3). This is expected: vetoes only prevent a subset of bad primitives; they do not provide a positive control skeleton. GBT supplies that skeleton by restricting decisions to log-grounded successors, turning “what to do next” from unconstrained generation into an executable policy over reusable macros.

Safety becomes a monotone, testable artifact.

Because gates are deterministic predicates over structured fields and are updated under experience-grounded monotonicity (Sec. 2.1), safety knowledge accumulates as a non-regressing library rather than an implicit prompt convention. This sharply reduces the attack surface of prompt injection and summary manipulation: summaries can affect macro realization, but cannot change ctx nor gate outcomes.

Robustness and efficiency share the same cause.

Spine memory eliminates transcript replay and constrains context to the visited macro path (Sec. 2.5), reducing both drift (fewer opportunities for compounding deviations) and cost (less context, fewer deliberation tokens). Recovery further converts stalls into progress by explicitly searching for feasible, low-risk macro paths instead of relying on free-form replanning.

Decoupling reasoning from execution is a system property.

The executor gains with 8B models (Sec. 3.5) are not “small-model magic”; they arise because GBT externalizes long-horizon structure and safety into an artifact that can be audited, versioned, and deployed independently of weights.

O.3 Future Work

Expanding coverage without weakening guarantees.

We see three complementary directions: (i) richer log mining to discover macros with higher compositionality; (ii) hierarchical composition of subtrees across task families while preserving the “no merge into gated nodes” discipline; and (iii) adaptive routing that can abstain early yet still propose safe, bounded exploration policies that are themselves externalized and testable.

More expressive yet verifiable safety.

A key challenge is extending beyond bounded-history ctx while retaining determinism and auditability. Promising routes include typed tool schemas with information-flow constraints, lightweight temporal logic over structured event streams, and synthesis of minimal counterexample traces that produce human-reviewable gate patches.

Continuous deployment with certified non-regression.

Self-evolution currently preserves safety by forbidding gate relaxation and regression-testing historical successes/unsafe corpora (Sec. 2.4). Future work can formalize this into deployment pipelines: signed gate libraries, reproducible replay suites, canary rollouts, and automatic “safety diff” reports that explain exactly which structured contexts became newly blocked.

Beyond benchmarks.

Bridging to open-world environments requires aligning 𝒮spec\mathcal{S}_{\text{spec}} with operational policies, measuring distribution shift for both behavior and safety, and integrating human oversight at the right abstraction level (macro and gate libraries) rather than at the level of raw transcripts.
